did_you_know.text: Did you know? Jeremiah 15 presents a decree so severe that even Moses and Samuel—known as leaders and intercessors for the people—would not be able to revoke it. The LORD says, “I have no pleasure in this people.”

Did you know? The people are given four possible fates: death, the sword, famine, or captivity. In this way, the chapter emphasizes that there is no escape from judgment—only different forms of calamity.

Did you know? The LORD describes four agents of destruction that will act against the people: the sword will kill, dogs will drag away the dead, and the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth will eat and destroy them.

Did you know? Jerusalem will become “a horror” to all the kingdoms of the earth “because of Manasseh son of Hezekiah, king of Judah.” The chapter connects the disaster to the actions of a king from the past as well.

Did you know? The LORD compares the scattering of the people to winnowing with a winnowing fork: “I scattered them with a winnowing fork.” The image conveys dispersion and loss, and it is immediately followed by the statement that the people did not turn from their ways.

Did you know? The figure of “the woman who bore seven” serves in the chapter as a symbol of national disaster: she loses her life, and the sun sets while it is still day—a picture of suddenness, shame, and destruction.

Did you know? Jeremiah describes himself as “a man of strife and a man of contention to the whole land,” even though he declares that he has neither lent nor borrowed at interest. His complaint expresses the social cost of his prophetic mission.

Did you know? Jeremiah describes the words of the LORD as though he found them and ate them; he says they became “the joy and delight of my heart.” The image expresses how deeply he internalized the prophecy.

Did you know? The LORD requires Jeremiah to return and stand before Him, bringing out “the precious from the worthless”—distinguishing what is worthy from what is unworthy in his words and mission. In return, He promises that the people will turn to Jeremiah, but he will not turn to them.
Did you know? The LORD promises to make Jeremiah “a fortified wall of bronze”: his enemies will fight against him but will not prevail, because the LORD will be with him to save and deliver him.
